common_name: Great Wall Bamboo (Heat-Tolerant Dragon Head Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil; give afternoon shade the first summer to ease establishment in hot climates.

directions: This selection was bred specifically to overcome the biggest weakness of the genus for southern gardeners: most Fargesia decline in prolonged heat and humidity, while 'Great Wall' holds dense, glossy foliage and steady culm production through Gulf Coast summers that would scorch other fountain bamboos. It keeps the tight, non-running clump habit typical of Fargesia, making it a safe choice for foundation plantings, screens, and borders where a running bamboo would be unwelcome. Give it morning sun with afternoon shade and consistent moisture, especially while establishing, and mulch well to keep the shallow root zone cool. It remains reliably root-hardy through winters well below zero once mature, so northern gardeners are not sacrificing cold tolerance for this heat tolerance.

planting.note: Set out in spring so roots have a full warm season to establish before the first winter cold snap.

directions: Native to the Goias interior of central Brazil, this Butia is prized by palm collectors for arching, recurved leaves that emerge with a distinct burgundy-purple cast before mellowing toward silvery blue-green with age, a color unlike any other cold-hardy feather palm. It forms a slow, solitary trunk clad in persistent old leaf-base stubs and stays notably compact compared with the larger Pindo Palm. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates heat and drought well once established but is somewhat less cold-hardy than Butia capitata or Butia odorata, so it suits the milder end of the Gulf Coast or a sheltered microclimate elsewhere. Small tart fruits follow the same jelly-making tradition as its Butia relatives.

planting.note: Set out in spring so roots have a full warm season to establish before the first winter cold snap.

directions: Native to the borderlands of Paraguay, northern Argentina, and southern Brazil, this is the smallest of the commonly cultivated Butia species, often staying trunkless or forming only a short, thick base topped with narrow, stiff, silvery-blue arching leaflets. Its diminutive scale makes it a useful accent or container palm where a full-sized Pindo Palm would overwhelm the bed. Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil, and expect very slow growth, especially in youth. It tolerates heat and drought well but is best suited to the milder, more tropical end of Gulf Coast plantings rather than areas with hard, prolonged freezes.

common_name: Modesto Windmill Palm (California Cold-Hardy Seed Strain)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown palms after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving a full growing season to establish before facing winter cold.

directions: This strain traces to decades-old windmill palms grown widely around Modesto in California's San Joaquin Valley, an inland climate of hot, dry summers and occasional hard winter frost, and offspring grown from that seed source have earned a reputation among palm growers for vigorous trunk formation and reliable performance outside the mild coastal climates where the species is usually planted. It tends to size up faster than typical nursery-grown Trachycarpus fortunei once trunking begins, forming a full, bold crown of large fan leaves. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water deeply through the first two summers; established specimens handle both Gulf Coast humidity and occasional drought better than more shade-adapted hardy strains. Remove spent fronds as they brown to keep the shaggy fiber-wrapped trunk tidy.

subcategory: upright running bamboo with restrained clumping habit

planting.note: Install a rhizome barrier before planting near structures or beds; spread is slower and more restrained than typical Phyllostachys, but the rhizomes still run.

directions: Narihira Bamboo forms tall, ramrod-straight culms flushed with purple-bronze while young, aging to olive green, held in a dense, upright grove that reads more like a tight clump than a spreading thicket thanks to its unusually short rhizome necks. It makes one of the best narrow, high screens available among cold-hardy bamboos and tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity noticeably better than the high-elevation Fargesia species often recommended for similar uses. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil, and thin out older culms periodically to keep the grove airy and showcase the colorful new growth. It is reliably hardy through zone 7 winters and shrugs off the wind and heat of a Gulf Coast summer.

planting.note: Install a shallow rhizome barrier where a crisp bed edge is needed; spread is slow compared with most running bamboos but still worth containing in formal plantings.

directions: Unlike most bamboos, this dwarf Japanese species carries broad, short, glossy dark-green leaves on zigzagging stems, giving it a texture closer to a leafy shrub than a typical narrow-leaved cane, which is why it is sold under the common name Ruscus-Leaf Bamboo. It forms a dense, low, weed-suppressing mass useful as a woodland-garden groundcover, foundation planting, or clipped low border in shaded Gulf Coast landscapes. Plant in part shade in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil; full Gulf Coast summer sun can scorch the broad leaves, so afternoon shade is preferable. Growth and spread are slow, so mass plantings fill in fastest when starting from close spacing.
